description: Energy costs, e-waste, data privacy, and UK laws protecting personal data and creative work.
content_html:
Why Technology Has Consequences

Every device you use, every app you run, and every file you upload has costs and consequences beyond its obvious function. These fall into three categories: environmental issues, ethical issues, and legal issues. Understanding all three helps you evaluate technology honestly — not just what it can do, but what it costs and what rules govern its use.

Environmental Impact: Manufacture

A digital device does not start its environmental life when you switch it on — it starts when its materials are extracted from the ground. Producing a smartphone, laptop or server requires mining rare earth minerals and metals such as lithium, cobalt, copper and gold. These mining operations can cause habitat destruction, water pollution and significant carbon emissions. The energy-intensive fabrication processes used to manufacture processors and circuit boards add further to the carbon cost. Every new device purchased represents environmental impact before the device is even used.

Environmental Impact: Energy Consumption in Use

Running digital devices and the infrastructure that supports them requires vast amounts of electricity. Data centres power the internet, cloud services and streaming platforms. They run continuously and require cooling systems — which themselves consume electricity and water — to prevent equipment from overheating. Individual devices (phones, laptops, televisions) consume energy throughout their lifetimes, and wireless network infrastructure (mobile masts, routers) requires continuous power to operate.

Key Fact

The four stages of a device’s environmental impact are: manufacture (mining, fabrication emissions), energy consumption in use (data centres, devices, networks), replacement cycle (how often devices are upgraded), and disposal (e-waste and toxic materials).

Environmental Impact: Replacement Cycle and Disposal

The rate at which consumers replace devices matters. When manufacturers design products to become outdated or to stop receiving software updates after a few years — a practice sometimes called planned obsolescence — they accelerate the replacement cycle. Each discarded device becomes e-waste (electronic waste). Devices contain hazardous substances including lead, mercury and cadmium. When sent to landfill, these substances can leach into soil and groundwater. Informal recycling in some regions exposes workers to toxic chemicals. Responsible disposal requires using official recycling or manufacturer take-back schemes.

Individuals can help by repairing rather than replacing devices, choosing refurbished hardware, and using official recycling and take-back schemes. Manufacturers can design products that are easier to repair, use more recycled materials, and provide software support for longer. Organisations can choose data centre providers that run on renewable energy or use waste-heat recovery. Technology can also reduce other environmental harms: remote working cuts commuting emissions, digital documents replace paper, and smart energy systems can optimise heating and lighting in buildings.

Ethical Issues: Privacy and Personal Data

Privacy is the central ethical concern of the digital age. Every time you use a smartphone, banking app or social media platform, data about you is collected — your location, browsing history, financial transactions and social connections. Most people value the ability to control what others know about them. Privacy is challenged when organisations collect data that goes beyond what is necessary, share it without consent, or use it in ways users did not expect.

Three key ethical questions arise around personal data:

  • Ownership — who owns the data generated by your activity online? In many cases, the platform that collects it claims ownership, even when it relates entirely to your behaviour and preferences.
  • Consent — have users genuinely agreed to their data being collected and used in specific ways? Long, complex privacy policies can obscure the scope of what users are agreeing to.
  • Misuse — data collected for one purpose (for example, measuring fitness activity) could be shared with insurers or employers and used to make decisions that affect a person’s life without their knowledge.
Key Fact

Three ethical dimensions of personal data: ownership (who holds rights over data you generate?), consent (have users genuinely agreed to how data is used?), misuse (can data collected for one purpose be used in ways that harm the person?). All three are addressed by the Data Protection Act 2018.

UK Data Protection Law

The Data Protection Act 2018 governs how organisations handle personal data. It incorporates the requirements of UK GDPR (the UK’s retained version of European data protection regulation). Under the Act, organisations must: collect data only for a specific, stated purpose; keep it secure; not hold it for longer than necessary; and give individuals the right to access, correct or request deletion of their own data. Failure to comply can result in significant fines from the Information Commissioner’s Office. The Act replaced the earlier Data Protection Act 1998.

Intellectual Property: Copyright, Patents, Trademarks and Licencing

When someone creates software, music, a logo or an invention, they have rights over that creation. Intellectual property law protects those rights. There are four types you need to know.

Copyright — protected in the UK by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988. Creative works — including software, music, images, films and written content — are automatically protected from the moment of creation. Copying or distributing copyrighted material without permission is illegal, even for personal rather than commercial use.

Patents — a patent gives an inventor the exclusive right to make, use or sell an invention for a limited period (typically 20 years in the UK). In return, the inventor publishes how the invention works. Patents can protect hardware designs and algorithms in some circumstances, but pure software ideas are generally not patentable in the UK.

Trademarks — a trademark protects a distinctive name, logo or symbol associated with a product or brand. Technology companies register trademarks to prevent competitors from using confusingly similar names or logos. Unlike copyright, trademarks must be formally registered and renewed to maintain protection.

Licencing — a software licence is a legal agreement between the rights holder and a user, setting out what the user may do with the software. A proprietary licence restricts copying, modification and redistribution. An open-source licence (such as the GNU GPL) permits users to view, modify and share the source code, subject to conditions. Using software outside the terms of its licence is a breach of copyright law.

The Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes it a criminal offence to access a computer system without authorisation. It covers three categories of offence: gaining unauthorised access to computer material (for example, logging into someone else’s account without their permission); gaining unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate a further offence (for example, accessing a network to commit fraud); and making unauthorised modifications to computer material (for example, installing malware or deleting data). A 2015 amendment to the Act increased maximum penalties and extended its coverage to attacks on computer infrastructure. Hackers can face imprisonment and unlimited fines under this legislation.
exam_tip_html: For Explain questions on legal issues, always state the law’s name and year, then explain what it prohibits or requires — a bare name earns no marks. For Discuss questions on environmental impact, structure your answer around the four stages (manufacture, energy use, replacement cycle, disposal) and include at least one way to reduce each impact. For questions on intellectual property, be precise: copyright protects creative works automatically; patents must be applied for; trademarks must be registered; licences are contractual agreements, not a form of IP protection in themselves.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Digital devices have environmental costs across four stages: manufacture (mining and fabrication), energy use in operation (data centres, devices, networks), replacement cycle (planned obsolescence), and disposal (e-waste with toxic materials).
  • Personal data raises ethical issues of ownership, consent and misuse; the Data Protection Act 2018 gives individuals rights over their data and imposes obligations on organisations. The Computer Misuse Act 1990 makes hacking criminal.
  • Intellectual property is protected in four ways: copyright (automatic, protects creative works including software), patents (registered, time-limited, protects inventions), trademarks (registered, protects brand identity), and licences (contractual terms for permitted use).

practice_questions.text: State the name and year of the UK law that gives individuals the right to request deletion of their personal data held by an organisation.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Data Protection Act 2018. Developing: Data Protection Act (year missing or wrong). Emerging: Any other act named.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'planned obsolescence' and explain one environmental consequence it causes.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Planned obsolescence is the practice of designing products to become outdated or to lose software support after a limited period (1), encouraging consumers to replace devices sooner than necessary (1); this increases the volume of e-waste generated (1); discarded devices contain hazardous materials such as lead and mercury that can leach into soil and groundwater if sent to landfill (1). Secure: Correct definition plus one environmental consequence clearly explained. Developing: Planned obsolescence described but consequence vague or not linked to specific harm. Emerging: Term used without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ethical concerns raised by organisations collecting personal data from users.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ownership — the platform that collects data may claim ownership even though the data relates to the user's personal behaviour; this raises the question of who has rightful control (1+1). Consent — users may not have meaningfully agreed to their data being used in specific ways; long, complex privacy policies can obscure what is actually being consented to (1+1). Misuse — data collected for one purpose (e.g. fitness tracking) could be shared with insurers or employers and used to make decisions that negatively affect the user (1+1). Award any two concerns fully explained. Secure: Two clear concerns with explanation. Developing: One clear concern explained; second is vague. Emerging: Privacy mentioned without explanation.

practice_questions.text: A software developer writes a new application. Identify the type of intellectual property protection that automatically applies to this software from the moment it is created.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering/Secure: Copyright. Developing: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (acceptable — identifies the correct law). Emerging: Patent or trademark (incorrect — these require registration).

Mastering: A legal agreement between the rights holder and a user that sets out the terms under which software may be used, modified or distributed (2). Secure: Mentions legal agreement and permitted use (2). Developing: Partial — describes a licence as 'permission to use software' without mentioning legal/contractual nature (1). Emerging: Vague description with no legal dimension (0).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that the benefits of collecting large amounts of personal data outweigh the ethical and legal risks involved.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Benefits — personalised services improve user experience; health monitoring data can improve medical outcomes; analytics can drive business efficiency and economic growth (two developed points). Risks — privacy breaches expose sensitive data; misuse of data by insurers or employers can cause real harm; individuals often lack meaningful consent; organisations may prioritise profit over user welfare; legal obligations (Data Protection Act 2018) can be difficult to enforce globally (two developed points). Evaluation — weighs both sides; reaches a justified position acknowledging trade-offs between social benefit and individual rights. Secure: Both sides addressed with development; evaluation present. Developing: One side well-developed; other side listed without development; evaluation absent or weak. Emerging: One-sided argument with little supporting reasoning.

knowledge_checks.q: Which UK law makes gaining unauthorised access to a computer system a criminal offence?
Which type of intellectual property protection requires formal registration and protects a brand's name or logo?
The Data Protection Act _____ replaced the earlier 1998 version and incorporates UK GDPR requirements.
Discarded electronic devices containing toxic materials such as lead and mercury are collectively known as _____.
Match each intellectual property type to its key feature.
right: Automatically protects creative works from the moment of creation
Gives exclusive rights over an invention for a limited period
Protects a distinctive name or logo associated with a brand

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Data Protection Act 2018?
flashcard_questions.a: UK law regulating how organisations collect, store and use personal data, incorporating UK GDPR.

flashcard_questions.q: What rights does the Data Protection Act 2018 give individuals over their own data?
flashcard_questions.a: The right to see, correct or request deletion of their personal data.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
flashcard_questions.a: UK law making unauthorised access to computer systems and modification of computer material criminal offences.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Computer Misuse Act passed, and when was a key amendment made?
flashcard_questions.a: Passed 1990; 2015 amendment increased penalties and extended coverage.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protect?
flashcard_questions.a: Creative works — including software, music, images and film — from copying without permission.

flashcard_questions.q: When does copyright protection begin for a piece of software?
flashcard_questions.a: Automatically, from the moment of creation — no registration required.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a patent protect, and for how long in the UK?
flashcard_questions.a: An invention; exclusive rights typically last 20 years.
A legal agreement setting out the terms under which software may be used, modified or distributed.
Designing products to become outdated or lose support quickly, encouraging earlier replacement.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is e-waste harmful when sent to landfill?
flashcard_questions.a: Toxic materials such as lead and mercury leach into soil and groundwater.

flashcard_questions.q: What environmental impact does manufacturing a new device have before it is even switched on?
flashcard_questions.a: Mining rare earth metals causes habitat destruction and carbon emissions from fabrication.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one ethical concern about data ownership.
flashcard_questions.a: Platforms may claim ownership of data generated by users' own behaviour.

glossary_terms.definition: The effects of digital technology on natural systems, including energy use, resource extraction, and waste at all stages of a device's life.
Questions about what is morally right or wrong in the development and use of technology, where reasonable people may disagree.
Issues governed by laws that set clear boundaries on what is and is not permitted when using or developing technology.

Large facilities housing hundreds or thousands of servers that store and process data for online services, cloud storage and applications, consuming significant electricity and requiring cooling systems.
The principle that individuals have the right to control what personal information about them is collected, held or shared, and by whom.

A manufacturing approach where products are designed with a limited useful lifespan, through physical failure or withdrawal of software support, encouraging consumers to replace devices sooner than necessary.

Discarded electronic devices and components — including old phones, laptops, televisions and circuit boards — that may contain toxic materials and contribute to environmental pollution when improperly disposed of.

UK law that regulates how organisations collect, store, process and share personal data. It incorporates UK GDPR requirements and gives individuals rights over their own data, including the right to see, correct or request deletion of it.
UK law that protects creative works including software, music, images, literature and film from being copied, distributed or used without the rights holder's permission.
UK law making unauthorised access to computer systems, unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences, and unauthorised modification of computer material all criminal offences.
A legal agreement that sets out the terms under which software or other intellectual property may be used, modified or distributed by others.
